n: A new message begins. As often in Jeremiah, the Lord teaches not only with words but with an object lesson drawn from everyday life.
The Lord sends Jeremiah down to a potter’s workshop, promising to speak to him there. Ordinary work becomes a classroom for revelation.

f.g: Workshops were likely in the lower part of the city, near water and clay—perhaps by the Potsherd Gate (19:2).

n: Jeremiah obeys and watches a craftsman shaping clay on his wheel.

f.g: Hebrew ’obnayim, literally “two stones”—a potter’s wheel of an upper and lower disk, turned by foot or hand.

n: The pot is flawed, but the potter doesn’t throw the clay away—he reshapes it into a new vessel. The point is hopeful: while clay is still soft, it can be remade.
Now the Lord explains what Jeremiah has just seen.
Israel is like clay in God’s hands. He has the right and power to reshape his people—but, as the next verses show, how he shapes them depends on how they respond.

f.w: as the clay is in the potter's hand

n: If God announces that a nation will be uprooted and torn down…

f.w: to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy

n: …and that nation repents, God will change course and not send the disaster. His warnings are invitations, not fixed fate.

f.g: In KJV usage, God “repenting” means relenting or changing a planned action; “evil” here means calamity, not sin.

n: Likewise, when God promises to build up and plant a nation…
…but it turns to evil and will not obey, he will withhold the blessing he promised. Covenant blessings depend on faithfulness—a principle of agency.
So the Lord tells Judah plainly: I am shaping disaster against you—but turn back now, every one of you, and make your lives good. The door is still open.

f.g: Hebrew yotser—the same word as “potter.” God is “potting” a disaster, a deliberate wordplay.

n: The people’s answer is chilling: “It’s hopeless—we’ll do what we want.” They have given up on change and chosen their own stubborn hearts.

f.g: Stubbornness, the hardened will of the heart.

n: The Lord says even pagan nations have never seen anything like it: his own “virgin” people—meant to be pure and devoted—have done something horrible.

f.g: A poetic name for the nation as God’s bride or daughter, stressing what she should have been.

n: Does snow ever leave Lebanon’s peaks, or do cold mountain streams dry up? Nature stays faithful to its course—but Israel has abandoned its true source.

f.g: Mount Hermon and the Lebanon range carry snow much of the year, feeding the Jordan and other streams.

n: They have forgotten God, burned incense to empty idols, and left the “ancient paths” for rough, unbuilt trails that make them stumble.

f.g: Emptiness—a common word for idols, which have no real power.
A road not built up or graded—an unmade, dangerous track.

n: The result will be a ruined land that passersby hiss and shake their heads at in shock.

f.g: Whistling or hissing in astonishment or scorn at a ruin.

n: God will scatter them like a scorching desert wind, and in their crisis he will turn his back to them, as they turned their backs on him.

f.g: The hot, dry sirocco from the desert that withers everything.

f.w: I will shew them the back, and not the face

n: Jeremiah’s enemies plot against him: “We’ll still have priests, wise men, and prophets without him—let’s attack him with words and ignore him.” They trusted religious institutions more than God’s living messenger.

f.g: Slander him, bring accusations against him.

n: Jeremiah turns to the Lord in prayer, asking him to listen to what his accusers are saying.
“Is good repaid with evil?” Jeremiah reminds God that he had once pleaded for these very people. Now they have dug a pit to trap him.

f.w: digged a pit for my soul
I stood before thee to speak good for them

n: In anguish, Jeremiah asks God to let the coming judgment fall on his persecutors. This is a raw, honest lament, like many Psalms—the Bible records his pain without endorsing every wish.

f.w: deliver up their children to the famine

n: He prays that cries of terror will be heard in their homes when raiders come, because they set traps for his feet.

f.g: A band of raiders or invading soldiers.

n: Jeremiah leaves justice with God, who knows their plots to kill him. Later revelation calls disciples to forgive, but this lament shows the real anguish of a persecuted prophet.
